title: Electron Ptychography in the Fresnel Diffraction Regime
content: Three models underpin ptychographic phase retrieval: a model for the beam’s interaction with the sample, a model for propagating the resulting exit wave, and a model for measurement of the exit wave by the detector [1]. In their original, simplest, and still widely applicable form these models are that the beam and complex sample transmission function are multiplied to approximate the exit wave, that the exit wave’s propagation to the far-field is modelled by a discrete Fourier transform, and that there is an exact correspondence between the intensity measured by the detector and the intensity of the wavefront that impinges on it. By changing these basic models, variants of ptychography seek to improve resolution, ease sample constraints, ensure robustness in the face of noise, and minimize data/computation requirements. Examples of such changes include extending the beam-sample interaction model to accomodate thicker samples via multislice [2,3], including background noise and Poisson statistics in the detector interaction [4] and, the topic of our work here, moving the detector from the far-field into the Fresnel regime of diffraction and updating the propagation model accordingly [5]. Whilst there is much still to learn about the relative capabilities and practicalities of ptychography in this alternative Fresnel propagation regime (e.g. resolution limits and spatial frequency response [6]), in our electron experiments we have focused on aspects in which it has already demonstrated itself highly capable: realizing high-precision, large field of view quantitative phase images from minimum data requirements [7-10].
